name: Agricultural Drones: UAS Technology and Maintenance
objectives: Given an agricultural drone system, name each main part of the aircraft and ground system and explain what it does, including the flight controller, sensors, C2 link and payload
With a set of drone batteries, describe how to charge, store, transport and retire them safely, following every safety step, with no swollen or damaged battery used
Given a camera, sensor or spray payload, describe how to mount, clean and check it, with the payload secure, optics clean and spray parts checked for wear

chapters.name: Chapter 1: How a farm drone system works

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The parts of a drone system
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Name the main parts of a drone system and explain what each does.
This lesson builds toward: Given an agricultural drone system, you will name each main part of the aircraft and ground system and explain what it does, including the flight controller, sensors, C2 link and payload.
Authorities call a drone a system (UAS or RPAS) because the aircraft is only one part. The system includes the aircraft, the ground station (controller, phone or tablet, software), the radio link between them (often called the command and control, or C2, link), batteries and chargers, and the payload (camera, sensor or spray system).
On the aircraft: the airframe (body and arms, or wings); motors and propellers that create lift; electronic speed controllers (ESCs) that tell each motor how fast to spin; the flight controller, the drone's brain; and sensors: GNSS (satellite positioning such as GPS), compass, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) that senses tilt and movement, a barometer for height, and often obstacle sensors.
The flight controller reads the sensors hundreds of times a second and adjusts each motor to keep the drone stable and on course. If one sensor gives bad data, such as a compass near metal, the whole drone can behave strangely. That is why calibration and careful take-off spots matter.
Words to know:
- Airframe: the body, arms or wings of the drone.
- ESC: electronic speed controller: controls how fast each motor spins.
- Flight controller: the drone's on-board computer that keeps it stable and on course.
- GNSS: global navigation satellite systems, such as GPS, used for position.
- IMU: inertial measurement unit: senses tilt, turning and movement.
- C2 link: command and control link: the radio connection between controller and drone.
Official sources:
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Take a drone (or a clear photo or diagram of one) and label at least eight parts: airframe, motors, propellers, flight controller location, GNSS module, camera or payload, battery, controller. Next to each, write its job in one line.
You can now name the parts of a drone system and say what each one does.

options: The pilot's hand controller
The drone's brain that reads sensors and adjusts the motors
The battery charger
The camera mount
check.why: The flight controller reads the sensors many times a second and adjusts each motor to keep the drone stable.

check.q: You are about to take off next to a metal water tank and the drone drifts strangely. What is a likely cause?
options: The propellers are too new
The payload is too clean
The battery is too full
Bad compass data from the nearby metal
check.why: A compass near metal gives bad data, and the whole drone can behave strangely.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Batteries: the part that needs the most care
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Charge, store, transport and retire drone batteries safely.
This lesson builds toward: With a set of drone batteries, you will describe how to charge, store, transport and retire them safely, following every safety step, with no swollen or damaged battery used.
Most drones use lithium-polymer (LiPo) or similar lithium batteries. They hold a lot of energy for their weight, which is why they can also catch fire if damaged, overcharged, over-discharged or overheated. Battery care is the most important maintenance job.
Charge only with the correct charger, on a non-flammable surface, never unattended, and never a battery that is swollen, punctured or hot. Let a battery cool after flying before charging, and let it cool or warm to normal temperature before flying. Do not leave batteries in a hot car or in direct sun on the field.
For storage longer than a few days, keep batteries at storage charge (partly charged, not full or empty; many smart batteries do this by themselves), in a cool, dry place, ideally in a fire-resistant bag or box. Track each battery's charge cycles and condition. Retire swollen or damaged batteries and dispose of them through a proper e-waste or battery collection point, never in a fire or ordinary rubbish. Carrying batteries on aeroplanes has its own airline rules.
Step by step:
- Number each battery and log its cycles.
- Charge with the correct charger, on a non-flammable surface, attended.
- Never charge or fly a swollen, punctured or hot battery.
- Keep batteries out of hot cars and direct sun.
- Store at storage charge in a cool, dry, fire-resistant container.
- Retire damaged batteries to a proper collection point.
Words to know:
- LiPo: lithium-polymer battery: light and powerful, but can catch fire if mistreated.
- Charge cycle: one full use of a battery's capacity, from charged to used and back.
- Storage charge: a partial charge level that keeps lithium batteries healthy when not in use.
- E-waste: electronic waste, which needs special collection and recycling.
Try it now: Write a one-page battery procedure for a drone team: numbering, charging, field handling in heat, storage, a cycle log and retirement. Add a battery log table with columns for battery number, date, cycles, condition and notes.
You can now charge, store, transport and retire drone batteries safely and keep a battery log.

options: Partly charged, not full or empty, for storage longer than a few days
Fully charged
Completely empty
Charged in a hot car
check.why: Batteries stored for more than a few days are kept partly charged in a cool, dry place.

check.q: You have just landed and want to fly again soon. The battery is hot. What do you do?
options: Charge it right away in the sun
Charge it in the car and walk away
Let it cool before charging, and charge it attended on a non-flammable surface
Put it in the freezer
check.why: Charging a hot battery or charging unattended raises the risk of fire.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Payloads: cameras, sensors and spray systems
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Handle, mount and look after the main agricultural drone payloads.
This lesson builds toward: Given a camera, sensor or spray payload, you will describe how to mount, clean and check it, with the payload secure, optics clean and spray parts checked for wear.
The payload is what the drone carries to do the job. Mapping drones carry an RGB camera, often on a gimbal that keeps it steady. Crop health drones may carry a multispectral camera with a sunlight sensor and a calibration panel. Thermal cameras measure heat. Spray drones carry a tank, pump, hoses and nozzles, and some spread granules or seed.
Look after the optics: keep lenses and the sunlight sensor clean with a soft lens cloth, protect them with caps, and keep cameras out of dust and moisture. Check that the gimbal moves freely and the payload is mounted tightly; a loose payload upsets the balance and the flight controller.
Spray systems need extra care: after each use they are rinsed and cleaned as the maker and pesticide label require, nozzles are checked for wear and blockages, and the whole system is calibrated so it applies the right amount. Remember that spraying by drone needs aviation and pesticide approvals; maintenance does not replace them.
Words to know:
- Payload: the equipment the drone carries to do the job, such as a camera or spray tank.
- Gimbal: a motorised mount that keeps the camera steady.
- Sunlight sensor: a small sensor on top of some multispectral drones that measures incoming light to correct readings.
- Nozzle: the tip that turns liquid into spray droplets.
Official sources:
- FAO and ITU: E-agriculture in Action: Drones for Agriculture (2018)
Try it now: Choose one payload (RGB camera, multispectral camera or spray system). Write a care checklist with at least six items for before and after each use.
You can now mount, clean and check the main agricultural drone payloads.

check.q: What is the payload on an agricultural drone?
options: The battery
The ground station
What the drone carries to do the job, such as a camera or spray system
The radio link
check.why: The payload is the camera, sensor, spray or spreading system that does the work.

check.q: After a spraying job, what do you do with the spray system?
options: Rinse and clean it as the maker and label require, and check the nozzles
Leave the leftover mix in the tank
Wash the whole drone with a water jet
Store it wet in the sun
check.why: Spray systems are rinsed and cleaned after each use, and nozzles are checked for wear and blockages.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Maintenance in the field and workshop

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Inspections before and after every flight
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a pre-flight and post-flight inspection and record what you find.
This lesson builds toward: Before and after each flight, you will run a pre-flight and post-flight inspection and record what you find, checking every item on the checklist.
Inspections catch small problems before they cause a crash. A pre-flight inspection checks that the drone is fit to fly now; a post-flight inspection finds damage or wear from the flight just done and sets up the next day.
Pre-flight: airframe and arms free of cracks, arms locked; propellers clean, tight and free of chips or cracks; motors spin freely without grinding; payload secure and lens clean; battery seated and latched; sensors and vision windows clean; controller and app ready; firmware status checked before leaving base.
Post-flight: let motors and batteries cool; check for heat in motors (an unusually hot motor may be failing); look for new damage, dust or grass in motors and vents; clean the drone with a soft brush or dry cloth (no water jets on electronics); note flight time, problems and any warning messages in the log.
Step by step:
- Pre-flight: frame, arms, propellers, motors, payload, battery, sensors, controller.
- Fly only if every item passes.
- Post-flight: cool down, check motor heat, look for damage and dirt.
- Clean with a soft brush or dry cloth.
- Log flight time, problems and warnings.
Words to know:
- Inspection: a careful check for damage, wear or faults.
- Firmware: the software built into the drone, controller and batteries.
Try it now: Write a pre-flight and a post-flight inspection checklist of at least eight items each for a mapping drone. If you have a drone, use them once and log the results.
You can now inspect a drone before and after every flight and record what you find.

check.q: What is a pre-flight inspection for?
options: Finding damage from the last flight only
Charging the battery
Updating the firmware in the field
Checking that the drone is fit to fly now
check.why: The pre-flight inspection checks that the drone is fit to fly before take-off.

check.q: During the pre-flight check, a motor makes a grinding sound when you turn it. What do you do?
options: Fly carefully
Do not fly; check the motor for sand, grass or damage
Add oil to the propeller
Fly a shorter mission
check.why: Motors should spin freely; grinding means a problem to fix before flying.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Scheduled maintenance, firmware and records
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a maintenance schedule by flight hours and calendar, and keep maintenance records.
This lesson builds toward: For one drone, you will write a maintenance schedule by flight hours and calendar, a firmware update routine and a maintenance log, with whichever-comes-first intervals and every log field filled.
Some parts wear out with use. Propellers, motors, bearings, gimbals, landing gear and spray pumps and nozzles need replacing on a schedule. The manufacturer's manual gives intervals; your operations manual sets your own schedule. Plan by flight hours (for example every 50 hours) and by calendar (for example every three months), whichever comes first.
Firmware updates fix bugs and add safety features, but an update can also change behaviour. Read the release notes, update before you leave base (not in the field), update the drone, controller and batteries together, and test with a short flight before real work.
Keep a maintenance log for each drone: date, flight hours, what was inspected, replaced or repaired, parts used, firmware version, who did it, and the result. Authorities expect operators to maintain aircraft and keep records; clients and insurers may ask for them too.
Step by step:
- Read the manufacturer's maintenance intervals.
- Write your schedule by flight hours and calendar.
- Plan firmware updates at base, with release notes read and a test flight.
- Keep a maintenance log for each drone.
- Keep spare propellers and common parts in stock.
Words to know:
- Scheduled maintenance: planned checks and part replacements at fixed intervals.
- Maintenance log: the record of all maintenance done on a drone.
- Release notes: the maker's description of what a software update changes.
Official sources:
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Make a maintenance schedule table for one drone with at least six items (propellers, motors, gimbal, landing gear, batteries, firmware), each with an interval in hours and in months, and start a maintenance log with one example entry.
You can now plan scheduled maintenance and firmware updates and keep a proper maintenance log.

check.q: What does "whichever comes first" mean in a maintenance schedule?
options: Do the work only every three months
Do the work at the flight-hour limit or the calendar date, whichever is reached first
Skip the work if the drone flies well
Do the work only after a crash
check.why: Planning by flight hours and calendar, whichever comes first, keeps parts from wearing out.

check.q: A firmware update appears while you are at a client's farm. What do you do?
options: Install it right away in the field
Update only the drone and not the controller
Turn off all updates forever
Wait, then update at base after reading the release notes and test with a short flight
check.why: Updates can change behaviour, so they are done at base, all together, and tested before real work.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Troubleshooting and African field conditions
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Diagnose common faults step by step and protect drones from dust, heat, rain and power cuts.
This lesson builds toward: Given a fault or harsh field conditions, you will troubleshoot step by step and protect the drone from dust, heat, rain and power cuts, grounding the drone when a safety fault repeats.
Troubleshoot one step at a time: read the warning message in the app, check the simplest causes first, change one thing, and test. Common faults: compass error (move away from metal, vehicles and power lines, then recalibrate if asked); weak GNSS (wait for more satellites, move away from tall trees); vibration or wobble (check for a damaged or loose propeller or bent arm); motor error (check for grass, sand or a damaged motor); short flight times (aging battery, heat or a heavy payload).
Dust and sand get into motors and gimbals: take off from a mat or tarpaulin, clean after flying and store in a closed case. Heat shortens battery life and can overheat electronics: shade batteries and the controller, fly in cooler hours, and give the drone rest between flights. Rain and humidity damage electronics unless the drone is rated for them: do not fly in rain, dry gear and store with moisture-absorbing packets.
Where power is unreliable, plan charging: a vehicle inverter or a solar charging kit, enough batteries for the day, and charging overnight at base. Know when to stop: if a fault repeats or affects safety, ground the drone and send it to the maker's service centre or a qualified technician.
Step by step:
- Read the exact warning message.
- Check the simplest causes first.
- Change one thing at a time, then test.
- Use a landing mat; clean and case the drone after dusty work.
- Shade batteries; fly in cooler hours; no rain flights unless rated.
- Ground the drone if a safety fault repeats.
Words to know:
- Troubleshooting: finding the cause of a fault step by step.
- Calibration: a procedure that resets a sensor, such as the compass, so it reads correctly.
- Grounded: not allowed to fly until fixed.
Try it now: Final task: write the maintenance program for one drone: parts list with jobs, battery procedure, pre- and post-flight checklists, schedule by hours and calendar, a troubleshooting table for at least five faults, and a maintenance log template with two example entries.
You can now troubleshoot common drone faults, protect drones in African field conditions, and run a full maintenance program.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Parts list Main parts are missing, or what they do is not explained. Every main part of the aircraft and ground system is listed with what it does. Notes which parts wear out and which need calibration. Battery care Charging, storage or retirement steps are missing or unsafe. Safe charging, cooling, storage charge, transport and retirement steps, with cycle tracking. Includes a fire plan for the charging area. Inspection checklists No checklist, or key items such as propellers and battery latch are missing. Pre-flight and post-flight checklists cover airframe, propellers, motors, payload, battery, sensors and log notes. The payload checks fit the drone's real job, such as mapping or spraying. Schedule and log No intervals, or the log is missing fields. A schedule by flight hours and calendar, a firmware routine, and a log template with two example entries. Intervals are taken from the maker's manual and the source is noted. Troubleshooting table Fewer than five faults, or no steps. At least five common faults, each with simple first checks and when to ground the drone. Adds steps for dust, heat, rain and power cuts on the learner's own farms. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the program and check it again.

check.q: What is the first step in troubleshooting?
options: Read the warning message and check the simplest causes first
Change several parts at once
Open the battery
Fly higher to test
check.why: Read the message, check simple causes first, change one thing and test.

check.q: You will fly all day on a hot, dusty farm with no power. What do you plan?
options: One battery and take-off from bare sand
Leave the batteries in the sun to stay warm
A mat for take-off, shade for batteries, cooler hours and enough charged batteries or a solar or vehicle charger
Fly without resting the drone
check.why: Mats keep out dust, shade and cooler hours protect batteries, and charging must be planned where power is unreliable.
